```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(ecoTemporalNet)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
library(knitr)
```

# Overview

This vignette builds temporal overlap networks from frog phenology intervals.
Each file is treated as one community in a single calendar year on a common day
scale. Separate sites and years before analysis if a file combines groups.

The interval constructor requires one interval per species. These data can have
repeated species records, so we use its daily `presence_matrix` interface. A
species is present whenever any of its recorded intervals is active. Overlapping
records are counted once, while gaps between separate episodes are preserved.

This assumes the intervals define continuous presence and that days outside
their union are absent within the analysis window. It does not establish absence
from missing surveys. For raw survey observations with unknown dates, use
`prepare_phenology()` instead of inferring intervals or replacing unknowns with zero.

# Load data

```{r load-data}
frog1 <- readr::read_csv(
  system.file("extdata", "frogcomtest1.csv", package = "ecoTemporalNet"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
frog2 <- readr::read_csv(
  system.file("extdata", "frogcomtest2.csv", package = "ecoTemporalNet"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
frog3 <- readr::read_csv(
  system.file("extdata", "frogcomtest3.csv", package = "ecoTemporalNet"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(head(frog1))
```

# Plot phenology

Repeated intervals for a species appear on the same species row.

```{r phenology-plot}
ggplot(frog1, aes(
  x = start_day,
  xend = end_day + 0.5,
  y = reorder(factor(species), -start_day),
  yend = factor(species)
)) +
  geom_segment(linewidth = 8) +
  theme_classic()
```

# Convert intervals to daily presence

Reuse `get_daywise_overlap()` to expand interval records. Combine repeated-species
columns by taking their union, and include intervening empty days so matrix rows
represent consecutive calendar days.

```{r interval-to-presence}
frog_presence_matrix <- function(intervals) {
  required <- c("species", "start_day", "end_day")
  if (!is.data.frame(intervals) || nrow(intervals) == 0L ||
      !all(required %in% names(intervals))) {
    stop("Supply a nonempty interval table with species, start_day, and end_day.")
  }

  expanded <- get_daywise_overlap(intervals)
  represented_days <- as.integer(rownames(expanded))
  days <- seq.int(min(represented_days), max(represented_days))
  species <- sort(unique(colnames(expanded)))

  presence <- matrix(
    0L, nrow = length(days), ncol = length(species),
    dimnames = list(as.character(days), species)
  )
  for (sp in species) {
    records <- expanded[, colnames(expanded) == sp, drop = FALSE]
    presence[rownames(expanded), sp] <- as.integer(rowSums(records) > 0L)
  }
  presence
}

frog_presence <- lapply(
  list(frog1 = frog1, frog2 = frog2, frog3 = frog3),
  frog_presence_matrix
)
```

Each matrix has one column per species, not per record. Its analysis window runs
from the first to last represented day. A common explicit study window is needed
for comparisons of seasonal coverage between communities.

# Build networks

```{r build-networks}
frog_networks <- lapply(frog_presence, function(presence) {
  create_temporal_network(presence_matrix = presence)
})
g1 <- frog_networks$frog1
g1
```

Edges point from earlier to later first presence. Equal onsets use earlier last
presence, then species name. This is a tie-breaking convention, not evidence of
biological precedence. For repeated episodes, direction uses first and last
presence across the whole window, while weights count only shared positive days.
All species remain in the graph, including isolates.

Plot directly with igraph so isolated vertices also appear:

```{r network-plot}
igraph::plot.igraph(
  g1,
  vertex.label = igraph::V(g1)$name,
  edge.width = igraph::E(g1)$weight / 5
)
```

For symmetric co-occurrence, use the undirected option:

```{r undirected-network}
g1_undirected <- create_temporal_network(
  presence_matrix = frog_presence$frog1,
  direction = "undirected"
)
```

# Metrics

The edge table provides pairs and their total shared days. This replaces
`calculate_edge_persistence(frog1)`, which requires one interval per species.
Graph-only persistence reuses the package's summary without inventing a continuous
species interval.

```{r network-metrics}
edge_table <- igraph::as_data_frame(g1, what = "edges")
knitr::kable(edge_table[c("from", "to", "weight")])
calculate_persistence_metrics(g1)
calculate_latency(g1)
calculate_avg_temporal_network_degree(g1)
calculate_node_temporal_degree(g1, mode = "total")
```

Graph-only average node persistence is `NA`: a first-to-last span would incorrectly
include gaps between episodes. Latency counts directed overlap steps, not elapsed
days. An isolated species has degree zero and cannot reach other species.

The original gap burstiness and latency-weighted memory calls are omitted here:
consecutive repeated-species records are not automatically a well-defined
species-level event sequence. The current latency-weighted memory function also
has the degeneracy described in its documentation. Define the event sequence and
its ecological interpretation before applying those statistics.

Summarize the other files with the same functions:

```{r community-summaries}
community_metrics <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(frog_networks), function(name) {
  g <- frog_networks[[name]]
  data.frame(
    community = name,
    n_species = igraph::vcount(g),
    n_edges = igraph::ecount(g),
    mean_degree = calculate_avg_temporal_network_degree(g),
    mean_overlap_days = calculate_persistence_metrics(g)$avg_edge_persistence
  )
}))
rownames(community_metrics) <- NULL
knitr::kable(community_metrics)
```

These are descriptive summaries, not tests of community differences. Consider
species pools, study windows and survey effort before interpreting differences.
